ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Participants gave informed consent before the experiment and received financial compensation.
In the symmetrical audio-visual (SymAV) condition, the cameras for both participants were turned on, allowing them to see each other.
In the audio-only (AO) condition, the cameras for both participants were turned off.
Pairs of participants were brought to two separate experiment rooms to perform a director-matcher repeated referential communication task on Zoom.
At the beginning of the task, participants were asked to stand in front of the screens and wear headphones connected to the upper monitor.

Participants were then allowed to ask questions, which was followed by the explanation of the visibility condition (e.g., AsymAV condition participant B: You can see your partner [experimenter pointing at the main view], but your partner cannot see you [experimenter pointing at the self-view]).
Participants completed 96 trials (16 trials x 6 rounds) in the assigned condition while alternating the roles of director and matcher after each trial.

We found that speaker visibility is associated with the rate of referential alignment in gestures: Participants were more likely to align with their conversation partner's gestures if they could see their partner's gestures (SymAV and AsymAV) compared to when they could not see each other (AO), but the visibility of their own gestures to their partner did not affect the rate of referentially aligned gestures (SymAV = AsymAV > AO).
table.formatted: We found that speaker visibility is associated with the rate of referential alignment in gestures: Participants were more likely to align with their conversation partner's gestures if they could see their partner's gestures (SymAV and AsymAV) compared to when they could not see each other (AO), but the visibility of their own gestures to their partner did not affect the rate of referentially aligned gestures (SymAV = AsymAV > AO).
table.header: 4.1. Seeing gesture primes the production of referentially aligned gestures

table.text: As participants had to communicate about 16 objects in each round, the priming effect on the gesture form may have faded away by the time they had to describe the object (see Appendix A).
table.header: 4.2. Seeing gestures may not affect gesture form alignment

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Participants gave informed consent before the experiment and received financial compensation.

> In the symmetrical audio-visual (SymAV) condition, the cameras for both participants were turned on, allowing them to see each other.

> In the audio-only (AO) condition, the cameras for both participants were turned off.

> Pairs of participants were brought to two separate experiment rooms to perform a director-matcher repeated referential communication task on Zoom.

> At the beginning of the task, participants were asked to stand in front of the screens and wear headphones connected to the upper monitor.

> Participants were then allowed to ask questions, which was followed by the explanation of the visibility condition (e.g., AsymAV condition participant B: You can see your partner [experimenter pointing at the main view], but your partner cannot see you [experimenter pointing at the self-view]).

> Participants completed 96 trials (16 trials x 6 rounds) in the assigned condition while alternating the roles of director and matcher after each trial.

> We found that speaker visibility is associated with the rate of referential alignment in gestures: Participants were more likely to align with their conversation partner's gestures if they could see their partner's gestures (SymAV and AsymAV) compared to when they could not see each other (AO), but the visibility of their own gestures to their partner did not affect the rate of referentially aligned gestures (SymAV = AsymAV > AO).

> As participants had to communicate about 16 objects in each round, the priming effect on the gesture form may have faded away by the time they had to describe the object (see Appendix A).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 7 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: compiled Python files (6), R history (1). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 934 columns across 32 data files.
#### Issues Identified

170 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 32 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Participants gave informed consent before the experiment and received financial compensation.
In the symmetrical audio-visual (SymAV) condition, the cameras for both participants were turned on, allowing them to see each other.
In the audio-only (AO) condition, the cameras for both participants were turned off.
Pairs of participants were brought to two separate experiment rooms to perform a director-matcher repeated referential communication task on Zoom.
At the beginning of the task, participants were asked to stand in front of the screens and wear headphones connected to the upper monitor.

Participants were then allowed to ask questions, which was followed by the explanation of the visibility condition (e.g., AsymAV condition participant B: You can see your partner [experimenter pointing at the main view], but your partner cannot see you [experimenter pointing at the self-view]).
Participants completed 96 trials (16 trials x 6 rounds) in the assigned condition while alternating the roles of director and matcher after each trial.

We found that speaker visibility is associated with the rate of referential alignment in gestures: Participants were more likely to align with their conversation partner's gestures if they could see their partner's gestures (SymAV and AsymAV) compared to when they could not see each other (AO), but the visibility of their own gestures to their partner did not affect the rate of referentially aligned gestures (SymAV = AsymAV > AO).
As participants had to communicate about 16 objects in each round, the priming effect on the gesture form may have faded away by the time they had to describe the object (see Appendix A).

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 8 R code files.
#### Run order

A dependency **cycle** was detected among 2 files (gestural_alignment_speakerB.Rmd, gestural_alignment_speakerB.R): each reads a file another writes, so no run order satisfies all of them. This must be resolved before the code can run.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:6, File = c("causal_inference.R", "causal_inference.Rmd", 
"preprocessing.R", "preprocessing.Rmd", "dtw_similarity_speakerB.R", 
"dtw_similarity_speakerB.Rmd"), "Runs after" = c("—", "—", 
"—", "—", "preprocessing.Rmd, preprocessing.R, causal_inference.R", 
"preprocessing.Rmd, preprocessing.R, causal_inference.Rmd"), 
    Basis = c("none", "none", "none", "none", "dependency", "dependency"
    )), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 8 scripts: 4 ran without error, 4 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **2 scripts use an object or function that only another script defines**, so in the second run that script was loaded first, in the same session: `dtw_similarity_speakerB.R` after `causal_inference.R`; `dtw_similarity_speakerB.Rmd` after `causal_inference.Rmd`. Such a script should `source()` the other itself, since it does not run on its own. 

*a script hit an `object '...' not found` error, indicating it expected a variable another script defines. We inferred which script supplies it and re-ordered so that script runs first, and re-ran once. The outcomes above are from that corrected run.*

text.text: People often align with one another's sentence structures, lexical choices, and co-speech gestures during conversation.
Such linguistic alignment has been attributed to both low-level priming and high-level collaborative efforts to establish mutual understanding (grounding).
Although the contributions of these processes have been extensively investigated for verbal aspects of language use, their roles in co-speech gestural alignment remain largely unexplored.

Here, we manipulated partner visibility in a video-mediated dyadic referential communication game (𝑛 = 45 dyads) to examine (i) whether priming and grounding contribute to the two dimensions of gestural alignment: referential and form alignment, and (ii) how lexical alignment relates to gestural alignment.

We found that participants produced referentially aligned gestures more frequently when they could see their partner's gestures than when they could not, irrespective of whether their own gestures were visible to their partner.
This pattern provides evidence consistent with priming, but not with the predicted grounding effect.

By contrast, visibility had little to no effect on Dynamic Time Warping (DTW)-based gesture form similarity, suggesting that the contributions of priming and grounding may differ between referential and form alignment.
Furthermore, lexical alignment was positively associated with the frequency of referentially aligned gestures, even after accounting for control variables.
This association is consistent with the possibility that shared conceptualization of referents contributes to gestural alignment.

Taken together, these findings highlight that mechanisms underlying alignment may differ depending on the dimensions of gestural alignment and point to distinct roles for priming and shared conceptualization in the alignment of co-speech gestures.
In social interactions, people coordinate their actions.
One aspect of interactive coordination is behavioral alignment-a tendency for people to repeat aspects of each other's communicative behavior (e.g., Pickering & Garrod, 2004; Rasenberg et al., 2020).
text.formatted: One aspect of interactive coordination is behavioral alignment-a tendency for people to repeat aspects of each other's communicative behavior (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Pickering & Garrod, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Rasenberg et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Alignment has been observed in a wide variety of behaviors, from less communicative behaviors such as foot-shaking and face rubbing (Chartrand & Bargh, 1999) to more communicative ones, including sentence structures (Branigan et al., 2000; Levelt & Kelter, 1982), word choices (Brennan & Clark, 1996; Clark & Wilkes-Gibbs, 1986), and co-speech gestures (Holler & Wilkin, 2011; Kimbara, 2006; Rasenberg et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Alignment has been observed in a wide variety of behaviors, from less communicative behaviors such as foot-shaking and face rubbing <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Chartrand & Bargh, 1999)</ref> to more communicative ones, including sentence structures <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Branigan et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Levelt & Kelter, 1982)</ref>, word choices <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Brennan & Clark, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Clark & Wilkes-Gibbs, 1986)</ref>, and co-speech gestures <ref type="bibr">(Holler & Wilkin, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Kimbara, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Rasenberg et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Understanding the cognitive and social processes underlying linguistic alignment in speech and, more recently, co-speech gestures has been an important research objective in psycholinguistics and cognitive science (Clark & Brennan, 1991; Fusaroli et al., 2014; Gandolfi et al., 2022; Holler & Wilkin, 2011; Kopp & Bergmann, 2013; Pickering & Garrod, 2004; 2021; Rasenberg et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Understanding the cognitive and social processes underlying linguistic alignment in speech and, more recently, co-speech gestures has been an important research objective in psycholinguistics and cognitive science <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Clark & Brennan, 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Fusaroli et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Gandolfi et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Holler & Wilkin, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Kopp & Bergmann, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Pickering & Garrod, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Rasenberg et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In interactive contexts such as conversation, linguistic alignment in speech and gestures has been proposed to arise from low-level priming processes (e.g., Pickering & Garrod, 2004) as well as grounding, a process in which speakers coordinate their communicative behavior to establish mutual understanding (e.g., Clark & Brennan, 1991).
text.formatted: In interactive contexts such as conversation, linguistic alignment in speech and gestures has been proposed to arise from low-level priming processes (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Pickering & Garrod, 2004)</ref> as well as grounding, a process in which speakers coordinate their communicative behavior to establish mutual understanding (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Clark & Brennan, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: In this paper, we aim to further our understanding of the mechanisms of linguistic alignment-particularly in co-speech gestures-by (i) experimentally assessing the effects of priming and grounding processes on gestural alignment, at the levels of meaning (referential alignment) and form (similarity of referentially aligned gestures' forms), and (ii) exploring the link between alignment in speech and co-speech gestures.
We also entertain the possibility of other mechanisms beyond priming and grounding.

One well-studied form of linguistic alignment is lexical alignment, also known as lexical entrainment, which refers to a tendency for people to use the same words when they repeatedly refer to the same objects (Brennan & Clark, 1996).
text.formatted: One well-studied form of linguistic alignment is lexical alignment, also known as lexical entrainment, which refers to a tendency for people to use the same words when they repeatedly refer to the same objects <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Brennan & Clark, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Consider the scenario where your conversational partner describes an object (see Figure 1), and your task is to find the target object through free communication.
text.formatted: Consider the scenario where your conversational partner describes an object (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>), and your task is to find the target object through free communication.

text.text: To experience lexical alignment first-hand, let's try to figure out the target object based on your partner's description (A).
(A) This object looks like a cup with a binocular on the left, and on the top, you see a stick attached to it.
You have probably correctly identified the leftmost object as the target.
Having performed the same task for the other four objects, now it's your turn to describe the same object to your partner.
How would you describe the object?
If you remember your partner's previous description, you would probably say something like "This is the object with the binocular on the left."

Here, you have reused or aligned the expression "binocular on the left" to optimize your description; the description has been halved but is still sufficient for your partner to identify the target correctly.

Such repetition of lexical items in referential communication was observed in Brennan and Clark (1996), and the authors proposed that, in order to increase the efficiency of references, participants establish a dyad-specific shared conceptualization of the objects (i.e., conceptual pact) and repeatedly appeal to it throughout the interaction, during which the conceptual pact can be further simplified.
text.formatted: Such repetition of lexical items in referential communication was observed in <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Brennan and Clark (1996)</ref>, and the authors proposed that, in order to increase the efficiency of references, participants establish a dyad-specific shared conceptualization of the objects (i.e., conceptual pact) and repeatedly appeal to it throughout the interaction, during which the conceptual pact can be further simplified.

text.text: In the case of our example, your conversation partner used a key expression, "binocular on the left," and you proposed the expression as a conceptual pact by reusing it.

In the next round, your conversation partner can signal agreement to establish the expression as a conceptual pact by repeating it in their description (e.g., The next one is the object with the binocular on the left).
As you repeat the process, you can simplify the conceptual pacts and shorten the description, as in "This is the binocular".
Alignment has been observed not only at the lexical level but also at other linguistic levels.

For example, Levelt and Kelter (1982) demonstrated lexico-syntactic alignment by showing that when store clerks were asked on the telephone about the opening hours with a prepositional phrase ("At what time does your shop close?"), they were 1.5 times more likely to answer with a prepositional phrase (e.g., "At five o'clock") than when the question did not contain a preposition ("What time does your shop close?").
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Levelt and Kelter (1982)</ref> demonstrated lexico-syntactic alignment by showing that when store clerks were asked on the telephone about the opening hours with a prepositional phrase ("At what time does your shop close?"), they were 1.5 times more likely to answer with a prepositional phrase (e.g., "At five o'clock") than when the question did not contain a preposition ("What time does your shop close?").

text.text: They also found that question-answer pairs were judged as more natural when their structures matched.

More recent studies have also observed syntactic alignment in controlled, monologue experimental settings (Corley & Scheepers, 2002; Ivanova et al., 2020) and in interactive settings (Branigan et al., 2000; Cleland & Pickering, 2003; Fusaroli et al., 2023; Hartsuiker et al., 2008; Ivanova et al., 2020), although some studies reported only chance-level syntactic alignment (Howes et al., 2010).
text.formatted: More recent studies have also observed syntactic alignment in controlled, monologue experimental settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Corley & Scheepers, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Ivanova et al., 2020)</ref> and in interactive settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Branigan et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Cleland & Pickering, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Fusaroli et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Hartsuiker et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Ivanova et al., 2020)</ref>, although some studies reported only chance-level syntactic alignment <ref type="bibr">(Howes et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Alignment also occurs in co-speech gestures.

In a director-matcher referential communication task, participants in the face-to-face condition mimicked more iconic gestures (i.e., co-speech gestures that depict concrete entities and/or actions; McNeill, 2005) than in the screen condition, where participants could not see each other (Holler & Wilkin, 2011). Oben and Brône (2016) contrasted the lexical and gestural alignment rates between the real interactions and shuffled, fictive interactions and demonstrated significantly higher rates of lexical and gestural alignment in the real interaction than in the baseline fictive interaction.
text.formatted: In a director-matcher referential communication task, participants in the face-to-face condition mimicked more iconic gestures (i.e., co-speech gestures that depict concrete entities and/or actions; <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">McNeill, 2005)</ref> than in the screen condition, where participants could not see each other <ref type="bibr">(Holler & Wilkin, 2011)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Oben and Brône (2016)</ref> contrasted the lexical and gestural alignment rates between the real interactions and shuffled, fictive interactions and demonstrated significantly higher rates of lexical and gestural alignment in the real interaction than in the baseline fictive interaction.

text.text: They also investigated the relationship between lexical and gestural alignment and found no reliable correlation between them, suggesting that dyads who produced more lexical alignment did not always produce more gestural alignment.

Another recent study conducting an interactive task similar to that of Holler and Wilkin (2011) showed that the emergence of alignment is predominantly multimodal (i.e., lexical + gestural), and multimodal alignment tended to emerge earlier than unimodal alignment (Rasenberg et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Another recent study conducting an interactive task similar to that of <ref type="bibr">Holler and Wilkin (2011)</ref> showed that the emergence of alignment is predominantly multimodal (i.e., lexical + gestural), and multimodal alignment tended to emerge earlier than unimodal alignment <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Rasenberg et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, Akamine et al. (2024) followed up on the work of Rasenberg et al. (2022) and demonstrated that participants continuously align in word choices and iconic gestures throughout a director-matcher repeated reference task.

(2022)</ref> and demonstrated that participants continuously align in word choices and iconic gestures throughout a director-matcher repeated reference task.

text.text: Several other studies have also provided support for the idea that alignment occurs in gestures (e.g., Bergmann & Kopp, 2012; Chui, 2014).
text.formatted: Several other studies have also provided support for the idea that alignment occurs in gestures (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bergmann & Kopp, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Chui, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: In these studies, however, the definitions of gestural alignment varied.
This variation may partly reflect differences in the degree of conventionality between words and co-speech gestures (e.g., iconic gestures).
Whereas mappings between forms and meanings are generally conventionalized for words, iconic gestures allow for greater variation in how meanings are represented through form (Kita & Emmorey, 2023).
text.formatted: Whereas mappings between forms and meanings are generally conventionalized for words, iconic gestures allow for greater variation in how meanings are represented through form <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Kita & Emmorey, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, alignment can occur at different levels of gestures, including their meaning (e.g., referent) and form (Rasenberg et al., 2020).
text.formatted: As a result, alignment can occur at different levels of gestures, including their meaning (e.g., referent) and form <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Rasenberg et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, previous studies differed in the degree of form similarity required for gestures to be considered aligned.

For example, Holler and Wilkin (2011) considered two gestures aligned only if they (i) referred to the same referent, (ii) used the same mode of representation (e.g., depicting a cup by tracing its shape with an index finger or by molding its shape as if holding it), and (iii) exhibited similar overall forms.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr">Holler and Wilkin (2011)</ref> considered two gestures aligned only if they (i) referred to the same referent, (ii) used the same mode of representation (e.g., depicting a cup by tracing its shape with an index finger or by molding its shape as if holding it), and (iii) exhibited similar overall forms.

text.text: Oben and Brône (2016) adopted a similar operationalization, but did not explicitly measure overall form similarity, assuming that differences in modes of representation would correspond to differences in gesture form. Opazo et al. (2024) required gestures to share a referent and at least one of three formal features: hand shape, orientation, or movement.

text.text: In contrast, Rasenberg et al. (2022) required only that gestures refer to the same referent (i.e., the same subpart of the stimulus).

text.text: These differences across studies highlight the lack of a standardized operationalization of gestural alignment and the importance of explicitly specifying the criteria used (Rasenberg et al., 2020).

text.text: Furthermore, the possibility of alignment at different levels underscores the importance of examining alignment at both the referential and form levels, especially when investigating the mechanisms underlying gestural alignment.
So far, we have presented evidence for linguistic alignment across levels and modalities.
However, one question remains: What makes us repeat each other?
It has been suggested that there are two major mechanisms underlying linguistic alignment-priming and grounding (Kopp & Bergmann, 2013; Rasenberg et al., 2020; Wynn et al., 2025).
text.formatted: It has been suggested that there are two major mechanisms underlying linguistic alignment-priming and grounding <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Kopp & Bergmann, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Rasenberg et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">Wynn et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Priming accounts-largely based on the Interactive Alignment Model (Pickering & Garrod, 2004)-propose that alignment is motivated by low-level, automatic processes, and alignment at one level (e.g., lexical) enhances alignment at other levels (e.g., phonology, syntax, conceptual).
text.formatted: Priming accounts-largely based on the Interactive Alignment Model <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Pickering & Garrod, 2004)</ref>-propose that alignment is motivated by low-level, automatic processes, and alignment at one level (e.g., lexical) enhances alignment at other levels (e.g., phonology, syntax, conceptual).

text.text: For example, hearing a particular word automatically increases the activation of its form, meaning, and syntactic properties in the mental representation, which in turn primes the listener to produce the same word in the following utterances (Branigan et al., 2000; Cleland & Pickering, 2003; Corley & Scheepers, 2002; Dijksterhuis & Bargh, 2001; Pickering & Garrod, 2004; Rizzolatti et al., 2001).
text.formatted: For example, hearing a particular word automatically increases the activation of its form, meaning, and syntactic properties in the mental representation, which in turn primes the listener to produce the same word in the following utterances <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Branigan et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Cleland & Pickering, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Corley & Scheepers, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Dijksterhuis & Bargh, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Pickering & Garrod, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Rizzolatti et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: It is possible that priming also occurs in co-speech gestures, such that seeing a gesture activates its form and depicted referent in the mental representation, priming the addressee to produce a gesture that aligns in meaning and form in the upcoming utterances (Chartrand & Bargh, 1999; Dijksterhuis & Bargh, 2001; Kopp & Bergmann, 2013).
text.formatted: It is possible that priming also occurs in co-speech gestures, such that seeing a gesture activates its form and depicted referent in the mental representation, priming the addressee to produce a gesture that aligns in meaning and form in the upcoming utterances <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Chartrand & Bargh, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Dijksterhuis & Bargh, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Kopp & Bergmann, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: However, only a few observational studies have investigated priming effects on gestural alignment (Oben & Brône, 2016), and further experimental investigation is needed to establish whether priming occurs at the gestural level.
text.formatted: However, only a few observational studies have investigated priming effects on gestural alignment <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Oben & Brône, 2016)</ref>, and further experimental investigation is needed to establish whether priming occurs at the gestural level.

text.text: In contrast, grounding accounts argue that speakers strategically and collaboratively align their behaviors in the process of co-creating shared conceptualization (i.e., conceptual pacts) and establishing mutual understanding (Brennan & Clark, 1996; Clark & Brennan, 1991; Clark & Wilkes-Gibbs, 1986; Holler & Wilkin, 2011; Rasenberg et al., 2022).
text.formatted: In contrast, grounding accounts argue that speakers strategically and collaboratively align their behaviors in the process of co-creating shared conceptualization (i.e., conceptual pacts) and establishing mutual understanding <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Brennan & Clark, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Clark & Brennan, 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Clark & Wilkes-Gibbs, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Holler & Wilkin, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Rasenberg et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In other words, grounding accounts consider lexical and gestural alignment-along with other interactive practices such as interactive repair-as communicative resources for establishing mutual understanding.
In grounding accounts, the relationship between alignment across levels is more flexible (Rasenberg et al., 2020).
text.formatted: In grounding accounts, the relationship between alignment across levels is more flexible <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Rasenberg et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: For example, speakers may align in lexical choices but modify or partially misalign aspects of their co-speech gestures, or vice versa, to calibrate mutual understanding (Rasenberg et al., 2022).
text.formatted: For example, speakers may align in lexical choices but modify or partially misalign aspects of their co-speech gestures, or vice versa, to calibrate mutual understanding <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Rasenberg et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: A model that does not subscribe to priming or grounding accounts-the interpersonal synergy model-also takes a stance similar to grounding in that conversation involves a dynamic, complementary coordination of alignment at different linguistic levels and modalities (Fusaroli et al., 2014; Trujillo et al., 2023).
text.formatted: A model that does not subscribe to priming or grounding accounts-the interpersonal synergy model-also takes a stance similar to grounding in that conversation involves a dynamic, complementary coordination of alignment at different linguistic levels and modalities <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Fusaroli et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Trujillo et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Although it may appear that priming and grounding accounts are mutually exclusive, this is likely not the case.
An instance of alignment may be driven by automatic priming as well as strategic grounding processes, among others.

For instance, in the earlier example of lexical alignment (the binocular example), did you repeat the word "binocular" because you were automatically primed by your partner's description, or because repeating the keyword let you describe the object most efficiently??
Or could it be both?
This highlights the importance of understanding the extent to which these processes drive alignment.

Although priming and grounding are among the best-known alignment mechanisms, other factors also play a role in driving linguistic alignment (Rasenberg et al., 2020), such as conceptual commonality and linguistic or communicative conventions.
text.formatted: Although priming and grounding are among the best-known alignment mechanisms, other factors also play a role in driving linguistic alignment <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Rasenberg et al., 2020)</ref>, such as conceptual commonality and linguistic or communicative conventions.

text.text: First, people may come to use the same words and similar gestures because their conceptualization of the referent is similar (conceptual commonality; Dingemanse, 2015; Mol et al., 2012).
text.formatted: First, people may come to use the same words and similar gestures because their conceptualization of the referent is similar (conceptual commonality; <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Dingemanse, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Mol et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, if two English speakers in different cities were to describe the concept APPLE, they would both probably use words such as "red", "circle", "fruit", and "sweet", due to the similarity in their conceptual representations of the concept, without being primed by each other or strategically repeating each other's words.
Second, repetition of lexical choices and gestures, among others, can also occur due to linguistic or communicative conventions (Dingemanse, 2015; Wynn et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Second, repetition of lexical choices and gestures, among others, can also occur due to linguistic or communicative conventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Dingemanse, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">Wynn et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: For example, function words (e.g., the, I, to, and) are among the most frequently used words because they consist of a limited set of vocabulary required to form grammatical sentences, leading to frequent cross-participant recurrences of the words.
In addition, people may use the same words to refer to an object because of community-wide conventions (Dahan, 2025).
text.formatted: In addition, people may use the same words to refer to an object because of community-wide conventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Dahan, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, if two English speakers were to name a picture of a shoe, they would both say "shoe", a conventional label for the object.

Unlike spoken words, gestures differ in the degree of conventionality of form-meaning mappings, with some (e.g., emblems, beat gestures, pragmatic gestures) having more conventionalized forms than others (Kita & Emmorey, 2023).
text.formatted: Unlike spoken words, gestures differ in the degree of conventionality of form-meaning mappings, with some (e.g., emblems, beat gestures, pragmatic gestures) having more conventionalized forms than others <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Kita & Emmorey, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: For example, the thumbs-up emblem gesture is widely used to signify approval, agreement, or satisfaction because the form is conventionalized.

This is in stark contrast with iconic gestures, which do not typically have conventionalized forms and rely more on the resemblance between the form and meaning, which may vary across speakers (e.g., Kita & Emmorey, 2023; McNeill, 2005).
text.formatted: This is in stark contrast with iconic gestures, which do not typically have conventionalized forms and rely more on the resemblance between the form and meaning, which may vary across speakers (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Kita & Emmorey, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">McNeill, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: For example, one could depict a cup either by tracing its shape or by molding the shape as if one were holding it.

The distinct characteristics of each gesture type suggest that factors influencing form alignment in gestures may differ for each gesture type: form alignment in emblem gestures is likely driven more by communicative conventions, while form alignment in iconic gestures is likely driven more by conceptual commonality.
In sum, speakers may still align with each other's communicative behavior to some extent, even without priming or goal-directed mechanisms.

Lastly, theoretical accounts of alignment suggest that alignment in speech and alignment in gestures are related (Kopp & Bergmann, 2013; Pickering & Garrod, 2021). & Garrod, 2004), accounts that theorize gestures as part of, or as interfacing with, the linguistic system (e.g., de Ruiter, 2007; Kita & Özyürek, 2003; Zora et al., 2026) suggest that alignment in lexical representation may facilitate alignment in gestures, and vice versa.

text.text: Although Kopp and Bergmann (2013) also proposed that alignment in speech and alignment in gestures are likely integrated, they did not specify how alignment in the two modalities might interact.
text.formatted: Although <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Kopp and Bergmann (2013)</ref> also proposed that alignment in speech and alignment in gestures are likely integrated, they did not specify how alignment in the two modalities might interact.

text.text: As they noted, "A detailed discussion of the degree and kind of interaction between [language comprehension/production and gesture] systems is beyond the scope of this chapter. . . .
We note, however, that both modalities are likely integrated (or, intra-personally aligned) during interpretation as well as production as indicated in our model by the dashed arrows" (p. 103).
Although there is ample evidence that speech and co-speech gestures are integrated, the interaction between alignment in speech and co-speech gestures remains underexplored.

Moreover, empirical findings about the relationship between lexical and gestural alignment have been mixed (Akamine et al., 2024; Louwerse et al., 2012; Oben & Brône, 2016; Rasenberg et al., 2022), underscoring the need to further investigate how alignment in the two modalities is related.

text.text: In summary, further research is needed to build an integrated model of alignment that accounts for (i) the extent to which priming and grounding contribute to alignment for each linguistic level across modalities and (ii) how alignment in the vocal and bodily modalities interacts (Kopp & Bergmann, 2013; Rasenberg et al., 2020).

text.text: The present study investigates (i) the effects of priming and grounding on gestural alignment and (ii) the relationship between lexical and gestural alignment.
To this end, we conducted a repeated-reference game in which pairs of participants repeatedly communicated about novel objects via Zoom.

We manipulated partner visibility to examine whether gestural alignment is primarily influenced by seeing a partner's gestures (i.e., priming) and whether mutual visibility provides an additional contribution (i.e., grounding).

Given that iconic gestures allow for greater variation in form-meaning mappings, and that alignment can occur at both the level of meaning and form, we use gestural alignment as an umbrella term for two dimensions of correspondence between speakers' iconic gestures.

Referential alignment refers to whether a speaker produces an iconic gesture for the same referent (i.e., a subpart of the stimulus in our task) that their partner previously gestured about, capturing the meaning dimension of alignment.
Form alignment refers to the similarity between the forms of these gestures.
Here, we use a kinematic measure that quantifies gesture form similarity continuously, going beyond the categorical annotations used in previous research.
We address the following two research questions: • RQ 1: To what extent do priming and grounding drive referential and form alignment in co-speech gestures?
• RQ 2: Is gestural alignment associated with lexical alignment?
To address the first research question, we analyze the effects of speaker visibility on two dimensions of gestural alignment.

The meaning dimension corresponds to referential alignment, and we analyze the rate of referentially aligned gestures (i.e., pairs of iconic gestures produced by different speakers for the same referent), which was coded by hand.
The form dimension corresponds to form alignment, and we analyze the form similarity of referentially aligned gesture pairs.

We examine these two dimensions separately because the mechanisms underlying alignment may differ depending on the aspect being considered (Eijk, 2023; Wynn et al., 2025), and this allows us to ask not only whether priming and grounding contribute to gestural alignment but also at which level (meaning or form) they do so.
text.formatted: We examine these two dimensions separately because the mechanisms underlying alignment may differ depending on the aspect being considered <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Eijk, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">Wynn et al., 2025)</ref>, and this allows us to ask not only whether priming and grounding contribute to gestural alignment but also at which level (meaning or form) they do so.

text.text: To investigate the contributions of priming and grounding, we manipulate speaker visibility.
For speakers to be primed by a partner's gestures, they must see their partner's gestures.
Thus, priming can contribute to alignment when speakers can see their partner but not when they cannot.

Grounding, in contrast, requires mutual visibility: speakers must see their partner's gestures to respond to them, and their own gestures must be visible to their partner to serve a communicative purpose.
We therefore expect grounding to contribute to alignment only when both speakers can see each other.
Based on these assumptions, we created three visibility conditions (see Figure 2; details in Section 2.3).
text.formatted: Based on these assumptions, we created three visibility conditions (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>; details in Section 2.3).

text.text: In the symmetrical audio-visual (SymAV) condition, both participants can see each other, allowing both priming and grounding to contribute to gestural alignment.
In the asymmetrical audio-visual (AsymAV) condition, participant B can see participant A's gestures and may therefore be primed by them.
However, because A cannot see B's gestures, these gestures cannot contribute to mutual grounding in the same way as in the SymAV condition.
In the audio-only (AO) condition, neither priming nor grounding is expected to operate because speakers cannot see each other.

We focus on gestures produced by participant B because the availability of priming and grounding varies systematically across the three conditions for this participant: neither process is expected to operate in AO, only priming in AsymAV, and both processes in SymAV.
Comparing B's gestures across conditions therefore allows us to investigate the effects of visibility and, under our theoretical assumptions, assess the contributions of priming and grounding.

We formulate four hypotheses concerning the mechanisms underlying gestural alignment: • H1 (priming, referential alignment): Seeing a partner's gestures contributes to referential alignment in co-speech gestures through priming.
If this hypothesis holds, we predict a higher rate of referentially aligned gestures in the AsymAV condition than in the AO condition.
• H2 (grounding, referential alignment): Grounding contributes to referential alignment in co-speech gestures.
If this hypothesis holds, we predict a higher rate of referentially aligned gestures in the SymAV condition than in the AsymAV condition.
• H3 (priming, form alignment): Seeing a partner's gestures contributes to form alignment in co-speech gestures through priming.
If this hypothesis holds, we predict greater form similarity within referentially aligned gesture pairs in the AsymAV condition than in the AO condition.
• H4 (grounding, form alignment): Grounding affects form alignment in co-speech gestures, but we make no directional prediction.

Grounding could increase form similarity if speakers repeat their partner's gestures to display incremental understanding, or decrease it if speakers intentionally modify their gestures to calibrate or expand on the proposed conceptualization (Rasenberg et al., 2020; 2022).
text.formatted: Grounding could increase form similarity if speakers repeat their partner's gestures to display incremental understanding, or decrease it if speakers intentionally modify their gestures to calibrate or expand on the proposed conceptualization <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Rasenberg et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2022)</ref>.

text.text: We therefore predict a difference in form similarity between the SymAV and AsymAV conditions but do not predict its direction.
If both processes contribute to referential alignment, we predict the order of the rate of referentially aligned gestures to be: SymAV > AsymAV > AO.
text.formatted: If both processes contribute to referential alignment, we predict the order of the rate of referentially aligned gestures to be: SymAV > AsymAV > AO.

text.text: For form alignment, H3 predicts greater form similarity in AsymAV than in AO, whereas H4 predicts a difference between SymAV and AsymAV without specifying its direction.

We evaluate the hypotheses using Bayes factors: BF10 > 3 is taken as evidence in favor of the hypothesis, BF10 < 1∕3 as evidence in favor of the null hypothesis, and values between these thresholds as inconclusive (Lee & Wagenmakers, 2014).
text.formatted: We evaluate the hypotheses using Bayes factors: BF10 > 3 is taken as evidence in favor of the hypothesis, BF10 < 1∕3 as evidence in favor of the null hypothesis, and values between these thresholds as inconclusive <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Lee & Wagenmakers, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: To examine the relationship between lexical alignment and referential alignment in gestures, we estimate the association between the frequencies of lexical alignment and referentially aligned gestures while accounting for potential task-related confounds (e.g., round and role).
We formulate the following hypothesis: • H5 (lexical-gestural association): Lexical alignment and referential alignment in gestures are associated.
If this hypothesis holds, we predict that the frequency of lexical alignment will be positively associated with the frequency of referentially aligned gestures.

This hypothesis is motivated by the Interface Model (Kita & Özyürek, 2003), which proposes that speech and gesture are linked through conceptual representations, such that how speakers organize information in speech can interact with how they express that information in gesture.
text.formatted: This hypothesis is motivated by the Interface Model <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Kita & Özyürek, 2003)</ref>, which proposes that speech and gesture are linked through conceptual representations, such that how speakers organize information in speech can interact with how they express that information in gesture.

text.text: Moreover, it has been suggested that spreading of alignment across linguistic representation levels may occur across modalities (Pickering & Garrod, 2021), although this proposal remains to be tested.
text.formatted: Moreover, it has been suggested that spreading of alignment across linguistic representation levels may occur across modalities <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Pickering & Garrod, 2021)</ref>, although this proposal remains to be tested.

text.text: Based on these theoretical accounts, we expect lexical alignment and referential alignment in gestures to be positively associated.
>Methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Methods</head>

text.text: We analyzed data from 90 Dutch-speaking participants (73 women, 16 men, 1 unreported; 𝑀 𝑎𝑔𝑒 = 22.7 years, 𝑆𝐷 𝑎𝑔𝑒 = 3.2, range = 18-33).
They were randomly grouped into 30 same-gender dyads and 15 mixed-gender dyads, each consisting of two unacquainted participants.

Dyads were randomly assigned to one of the three visibility conditions: 15 to the symmetrical audio-visual (SymAV) condition, another 15 to the asymmetrical audio-visual (AsymAV) condition, and the remaining 15 to the audio-only (AO) condition.
Participants reported no language-related disorders.
Participants gave informed consent before the experiment and received financial compensation.
The sample size was chosen to be comparable to those of previous studies within each visibility condition.

Previous studies on gestural alignment in interaction have included between 8 and 25 dyads, with a median of approximately 15 dyads (Bergmann & Kopp, 2012; Chui, 2014; Holler & Wilkin, 2011; Oben & Brône, 2016; Opazo et al., 2024; Rasenberg et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Previous studies on gestural alignment in interaction have included between 8 and 25 dyads, with a median of approximately 15 dyads <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bergmann & Kopp, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Chui, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Holler & Wilkin, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Oben & Brône, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Opazo et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Rasenberg et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The numbers of stimuli (i.e., 16 objects) and rounds (i.e., 6 rounds) in our study were also comparable to or greater than those in previous studies using repeated-reference games, which analyzed 8-12 objects across 6 rounds (Holler & Wilkin, 2011; Rasenberg et al., 2022).

text.text: The current study is therefore among the largest in this area to date.
The repeated referential communication task used a set of 16 pictures of Fribbles-3D objects composed of a main body and 3-6 subparts (Figure 3).
text.formatted: The repeated referential communication task used a set of 16 pictures of Fribbles-3D objects composed of a main body and 3-6 subparts (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>).

text.text: They were generated from the original Fribbles (Barry et al., 2014) with modifications designed to increase variation in elicited names (Eijk et al., 2022; Rasenberg et al., 2022).
text.formatted: They were generated from the original Fribbles <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Barry et al., 2014)</ref> with modifications designed to increase variation in elicited names <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Eijk et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Rasenberg et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: To explore the influence of speaker visibility on gestural alignment, we manipulated participants' mutual visibility on Zoom as a between-subjects factor.
Although one could apply this manipulation in co-present interaction, it would feel unnatural, since we usually see each other in such settings.
Such a manipulation is more natural in the Zoom environment because participants can turn off their cameras, and often do.
In the symmetrical audio-visual (SymAV) condition, the cameras for both participants were turned on, allowing them to see each other.
In this condition, we expected both priming and grounding to drive gestural alignment for both speakers.

This was because seeing the partner's gestures would prime their own production of gestural alignment (priming), and they could also intentionally "mimic" their partner's gestures for communicative purposes (grounding).
In the asymmetrical audio-visual (AsymAV) condition, only the camera for participant A was turned on.
This created an asymmetry in visibility: while participant B could see their conversation partner, participant A could not.
In this condition, only priming would drive gestural alignment for participant B, because they could see A's gestures and could thus be primed by them.
By contrast, B's gestures were not visible to A, so strategically repeating A's gestures would not carry any communicative benefits.
As for speaker A, priming could not occur for gestures because participant B's gestures were not visible.
Also, A could not intentionally align with B's gestures because they did not see B's gestures.
In the audio-only (AO) condition, the cameras for both participants were turned off.

In this condition, neither priming nor grounding would drive gestural alignment for speakers A and B. This was because they did not see each other's gestures, so their production of gestures could not prime their partners.
Microphones were turned on in all conditions, allowing participants to communicate verbally.
Figure 2 illustrates the visibility conditions.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref> illustrates the visibility conditions.

text.text: We analyzed the rate and form similarity of referentially aligned gestures produced by participant B (i.e., a first gesture produced by speaker A, and a second gesture by participant B for the same referent).

We focused on analyzing participant B's gestural alignment because comparing B's gestural alignment production in the AO and AsymAV conditions allowed us to quantify the effect of priming, and comparing the SymAV and AsymAV conditions allowed us to quantify the effect of grounding and/or the interaction effect of priming and grounding.
Pairs of participants were brought to two separate experiment rooms to perform a director-matcher repeated referential communication task on Zoom.

Each room was equipped with two 50 x 50 cm or 40 x 60 cm front lights, a Canon XF205 video camera with a Sennheiser ME64 cardioid microphone, a height-adjustable desk, two 24-inch HP monitors placed on top of each other, a wired Sennheiser HD 200 Pro headphone connected to the upper monitor, and a button box connected to the lower monitor.
To maximize the quality of video recordings for kinematic analyses, we set the frame rate (FPS) and shutter speed to 50 FPS and 1/250, respectively.
The upper monitor was used to play filmed instructions and display the Zoom screen, and the lower monitor was used to present stimuli via the Presentation NBS software.
Fribbles were labeled with numbers for one participant and with letters for the other participant.
The Zoom meetings were established via a peer-to-peer connection rather than the default cloud-based connection for increased stability and security, as well as lower network latency.
At the beginning of the task, participants were asked to stand in front of the screens and wear headphones connected to the upper monitor.
The distance between the participant position and the upper screen was 115 cm, and the distance between the participant and the lower screen was 80 cm.
We placed the lower screen closer to the participants to ensure they could perceive the Fribbles clearly.
Next, the experimenter adjusted the desk height to position participants on the video screen properly.
After adjusting the desk height, participants read written instructions on the lower screen and then watched filmed instructions on the upper screen.
In the instructions, information on the task procedure and a visual illustration of the visibility condition were provided.

Participants were then allowed to ask questions, which was followed by the explanation of the visibility condition (e.g., AsymAV condition participant B: You can see your partner [experimenter pointing at the main view], but your partner cannot see you [experimenter pointing at the self-view]).
Participants completed 96 trials (16 trials x 6 rounds) in the assigned condition while alternating the roles of director and matcher after each trial.
The director's role was to describe the target Fribble surrounded by a red square, and the matcher's role was to identify it.
They were allowed to communicate in any way they wished.
Once the matcher was confident that they had found the correct target, they read the Fribble label out loud and pressed the button to proceed to the next trial.
The placement of the Fribbles on the screen was randomized for each participant and was shuffled at the beginning of each round.
The trial order was semi-randomized: we prepared 15 sets of trial orders, and each set was assigned to three pairs (one pair from each condition).
The interaction lasted 24.0 min on average (𝑆𝐷 = 4.3, range = 15.0-35.4).

text.text: In total, the annotation contained 150,903 (59,610 content) words.
We manually segmented the stroke phase of 11438 co-speech gestures in ELAN (version 6.4; Wittenburg et al., 2006).
text.formatted: We manually segmented the stroke phase of 11438 co-speech gestures in ELAN (version 6.4; <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Wittenburg et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: The stroke phase is the core part of a gesture and bears the meaning of the gesture (Kita et al., 1998).

text.text: The segmentation of gesture strokes was done for each hand without audio.

To facilitate gesture segmentation, gestures were first automatically segmented using a Transformer-based gesture segmentation model (Ghaleb et al., 2024b; 2024a) for 15 dyads (five dyads per condition) 1 .
text.formatted: To facilitate gesture segmentation, gestures were first automatically segmented using a Transformer-based gesture segmentation model <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Ghaleb et al., 2024b;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2024a)</ref> for 15 dyads (five dyads per condition) 1 .

text.text: Trained research assistants checked the automatic segmentation and corrected inaccuracies.
Gestures for the remaining 30 dyads were manually segmented without the help of the gesture segmentation model.
Next, we played the video with audio and coded the semiotic dimensions of each gesture in terms of iconicity, deixis, beat, and pragmatics.
For example, if a gesture visually depicted the physical qualities of a Fribble (subpart) or actions/motions related to a Fribble (subpart), we coded the iconicity dimension as 1.
As for the deixis dimension, we coded it as 1 if the gesture located entities and actions in (metaphoric) space with regard to a reference point.
We coded the beat dimension as 1 if the gesture had a beat-like property.
Lastly, if the gesture was used to help maintain the conversation and had similar functions as discourse markers, we coded the pragmatics dimension as 1.
We decided to code the semiotic dimensions of each gesture instead of categorizing it into a single gesture category because of the multidimensional nature of co-speech gestures (Gullberg, 2010).
text.formatted: We decided to code the semiotic dimensions of each gesture instead of categorizing it into a single gesture category because of the multidimensional nature of co-speech gestures <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Gullberg, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Of 11438 gestures, we coded 7758 as gestures involving iconicity (we will call these gestures "iconic gestures" hereafter).
For each iconic gesture, we coded its referent using the predefined Fribble subparts.
In the case of Figure 4, speaker A produced a one-handed iconic gesture depicting an action of holding a handle-like object, which referred to Fribble subpart 09C.
text.formatted: In the case of Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref>, speaker A produced a one-handed iconic gesture depicting an action of holding a handle-like object, which referred to Fribble subpart 09C.

text.text: Therefore, the gesture's referent was coded as 09C.
Similarly, we coded the referent of participant B's iconic gesture in the following turn, which resembled speaker A's gesture, as 09C.
Inter-rater reliability for gesture segmentation and coding was assessed to determine whether the coders had a similar understanding of how gestures should be segmented and coded.
For the reliability of gesture segmentation and semiotic dimension coding, the Staccato algorithm (Lücking et al., 2012) was used to compute the chance-corrected degree of organization (DO) scores.
text.formatted: For the reliability of gesture segmentation and semiotic dimension coding, the Staccato algorithm <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Lücking et al., 2012)</ref> was used to compute the chance-corrected degree of organization (DO) scores.

text.text: For the reliability of referent coding, the modified Cohen's Kappa (Holle & Rein, 2015) was used to compute chance-corrected reliability scores.
text.formatted: For the reliability of referent coding, the modified Cohen's Kappa <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Holle & Rein, 2015)</ref> was used to compute chance-corrected reliability scores.

text.text: Inter-rater reliability was substantial for gesture identification (mean DO score of 0.72 for manual segmentation, 0.78 for model-assisted segmentation) and iconicity coding (mean DO score of 0.68), and almost perfect for gesture referent coding (mean raw agreement = 85.3%, mean Cohen's Kappa = .84).
We defined lexical alignment as cross-participant repetition of single lemmas or sequences of lemmas containing at least one content word referring to the same target Fribble (Akamine et al., 2024).
text.formatted: We defined lexical alignment as cross-participant repetition of single lemmas or sequences of lemmas containing at least one content word referring to the same target Fribble <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Akamine et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: We considered the lemma of each word instead of its surface form because lexical alignment pertains to alignment in lexical choices (e.g., Brennan & Clark, 1996; Wynn et al., 2025), and previous studies investigating lexical alignment in annotation.
text.formatted: We considered the lemma of each word instead of its surface form because lexical alignment pertains to alignment in lexical choices (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Brennan & Clark, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">Wynn et al., 2025)</ref>, and previous studies investigating lexical alignment in annotation.

text.text: We selected an equal number of dyads from each visibility condition for model-assisted coding to ensure that differences in annotation procedure would not systematically affect comparisons between conditions.
conversation used lemmatized words for detecting lexical alignment (e.g., Chieng et al., 2024; Dideriksen et al., 2022; Fusaroli et al., 2017).
text.formatted: conversation used lemmatized words for detecting lexical alignment (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Chieng et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Dideriksen et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Fusaroli et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: We restricted our analyses to content words because they tend to be more meaningful and unique to each Fribble (subpart) than function words (Brennan & Clark, 1996; Hawkins et al., 2020).
text.formatted: We restricted our analyses to content words because they tend to be more meaningful and unique to each Fribble (subpart) than function words <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Brennan & Clark, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Hawkins et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: We imposed no restrictions on the timing of alignment: two expressions that refer to a particular Fribble were considered aligned regardless of the rounds in which they were produced, as long as the first expression was produced by one of the interlocutors and the second by the other.
This is because participants most likely repeat their partner's word choices when describing the target Fribbles, and the roles of director and matcher for each Fribble alternated round-by-round.

This means that lexical alignment most likely occurs across immediately adjacent rounds, and it is necessary to allow each element in aligned shared expression pairs to be produced in different rounds in order to capture the use of lexical alignment in repeated references.
To prepare data for lexical alignment detection, we preprocessed speech transcripts in Python to remove disfluencies, tag part-of-speech (PoS), and lemmatize each word (e.g., eating → eat).
We used the spaCy library (version 3.8.2; Honnibal et al., 2020) for the PoS tagging and lemmatization.
text.formatted: We used the spaCy library (version 3.8.2; <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Honnibal et al., 2020)</ref> for the PoS tagging and lemmatization.

text.text: Following a similar approach to Sinclair and Fernández (2021) and Ghaleb et al. (2024d), we then extracted all shared expressions, defined as sequences of lemmatized content words that both interlocutors used to describe the same Fribblefoot_1 .
text.formatted: Following a similar approach to <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Sinclair and Fernández (2021)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Ghaleb et al. (2024d)</ref>, we then extracted all shared expressions, defined as sequences of lemmatized content words that both interlocutors used to describe the same Fribble<ref type="foot" target="#foot_1">foot_1</ref> .

text.text: For example, if both speakers A and B used the word "handle" to refer to Fribble 09, we considered it a shared expression for that Fribble.
If both speakers used the word to refer to multiple Fribbles (e.g., Fribbles 9 and 14), we considered it a shared expression for each of those Fribbles.

However, if speaker A used the word only for Fribble 09 and speaker B used it only for Fribble 14, it was not counted as a shared expression for either Fribble, because the speakers did not use it for the same referent.

We required shared expressions to refer to the same Fribble to align our operationalization of lexical alignment with previous studies, which examined whether speakers used the same words when referring to the same target picture or event (e.g., Bergmann et al., 2015; Branigan et al., 2011; Oben & Brône, 2016).
text.formatted: We required shared expressions to refer to the same Fribble to align our operationalization of lexical alignment with previous studies, which examined whether speakers used the same words when referring to the same target picture or event (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bergmann et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Branigan et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Oben & Brône, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, we listed all instances of each shared expression per Fribble (e.g., all instances of "Pinocchio" for Fribble 09) and marked a pair of shared expressions as an instance of lexical alignment if the first shared expression was produced by one of the interlocutors and the next one by the other.
The final dataframe contained 5472 instances of lexical alignment.
Figure 4 visually represents the operationalization of lexical alignment.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref> visually represents the operationalization of lexical alignment.

text.text: >Gestural alignment coding
text.formatted: <head n="2.7." >Gestural alignment coding</head>

text.text: A referentially aligned gesture was operationalized as "a cross-participant repetition of iconic gestures produced for the same Fribble subpart" (Akamine et al., 2024; Rasenberg et al., 2020; see Figure 4 for an example of gestural alignment).
text.formatted: A referentially aligned gesture was operationalized as "a cross-participant repetition of iconic gestures produced for the same Fribble subpart" <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Akamine et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Rasenberg et al., 2020</ref>; see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref> for an example of gestural alignment).

text.text: As with lexical alignment coding, we did not restrict the timing of alignment: a pair of iconic gestures produced for the same referent can be considered aligned even if they were produced in different rounds.
We did not require the form of iconic gestures to be similar for them to be considered referentially aligned.
Rather, we analyzed the form alignment as a dependent variable.
A detailed description of the measure of gesture form similarity will be provided in the next section.
The operationalization of lexical and gestural alignment differs in terms of the level of form alignment required.
For lexical alignment, the lemma of the word must be identical, and referentially aligned words that do not share the lemma (e.g., rod and handle) are not considered lexically aligned.
In contrast, we considered pairs of gestures to be referentially aligned as long as they were produced for the same referent, regardless of the similarity in their forms.
We distinguished between referential and form alignment in gestures for two reasons.
First, while form-meaning mappings are conventionalized for lexical items, iconic gestures allow for greater variation in how a given referent is represented through form (Kita & Emmorey, 2023).
text.formatted: First, while form-meaning mappings are conventionalized for lexical items, iconic gestures allow for greater variation in how a given referent is represented through form <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Kita & Emmorey, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, copying the exact form of words is much easier than copying the exact form of iconic gestures, and imposing the same requirement for lexical and gestural alignment may overlook the fundamental differences between the vocal and bodily modalities.
Second, the study aims to test the effects of priming and grounding without presupposing either.
Grounding accounts argue that speakers may maintain the referent of a gesture while modifying its form to negotiate or calibrate mutual understanding (Rasenberg et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Grounding accounts argue that speakers may maintain the referent of a gesture while modifying its form to negotiate or calibrate mutual understanding <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Rasenberg et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: If we required gestures to share similar forms to qualify as aligned, we would miss those cases, making our measure less sensitive to the potential contributions of grounding.
By operationalizing referential alignment independently of form similarity, we aimed to capture these cases and examine whether priming and grounding also affect alignment in gesture forms.

To summarize, we considered a pair of iconic gestures to be referentially aligned if they shared the same meaning and were produced by different speakers, regardless of the rounds in which they were produced and of their visual resemblance to each other.
Instead of considering the gesture form similarity as a selection criterion for alignment, we analyzed it as another dependent variable.

Based on the hand-coded referent information, we automatically identified 1979 instances of referentially aligned gestures, of which 986 were established by speaker B. Figure 4 visually represents the referential alignment operationalization.
text.formatted: Based on the hand-coded referent information, we automatically identified 1979 instances of referentially aligned gestures, of which 986 were established by speaker B. Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref> visually represents the referential alignment operationalization.
