text.text: In the present study, we used Dynamic time warping (DTW) distance as an inverse measure of the similarity of referentially aligned gesturesfoot_2 .
text.formatted: In the present study, we used Dynamic time warping (DTW) distance as an inverse measure of the similarity of referentially aligned gestures<ref type="foot" target="#foot_2">foot_2</ref> .

text.text: DTW is an algorithm used to compute the distance (dissimilarity) between two sets of time series (Giorgino, 2009; Müller, 2007; Ratanamahatana & Keogh, 2004).
text.formatted: DTW is an algorithm used to compute the distance (dissimilarity) between two sets of time series <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Giorgino, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Müller, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Ratanamahatana & Keogh, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: In the context of gesture studies, DTW can measure how similar a pair of gestures is in terms of their forms (lower distance means higher similarity; Pouw and Dixon, 2019; Pouw et al., 2021a; 2021b; Sato et al., 2020; Schueller et al., 2017; Trujillo et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In the context of gesture studies, DTW can measure how similar a pair of gestures is in terms of their forms (lower distance means higher similarity; <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Pouw and Dixon, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Pouw et al., 2021a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">2021b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Sato et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Schueller et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Trujillo et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: It has been demonstrated that DTW distance scores moderately correlate with manual annotations of gesture form similarity, suggesting that DTW can serve as a proxy for gesture form similarity (Akamine et al., 2026).
text.formatted: It has been demonstrated that DTW distance scores moderately correlate with manual annotations of gesture form similarity, suggesting that DTW can serve as a proxy for gesture form similarity <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Akamine et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: We computed DTW distance for each pair of referentially aligned iconic gestures following the DTW pipeline introduced in Akamine et al. (2026).
text.formatted: We computed DTW distance for each pair of referentially aligned iconic gestures following the DTW pipeline introduced in <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Akamine et al. (2026)</ref>.

text.text: An asymmetric, multivariate DTW implemented in the dtw-python package (version 1.5.1; Giorgino, 2009; Tormene et al., 2009) was applied to preprocessed motion tracking data generated by MediaPipe (Lugaresi et al., 2019; Pouw & Akamine, 2025).
text.formatted: An asymmetric, multivariate DTW implemented in the dtw-python package (version 1.5.1; <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Giorgino, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Tormene et al., 2009)</ref> was applied to preprocessed motion tracking data generated by MediaPipe <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Lugaresi et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Pouw & Akamine, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Figure 5 shows the normalized DTW distance for a similar and less similar referentially aligned gesture pair.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">5</ref> shows the normalized DTW distance for a similar and less similar referentially aligned gesture pair.

text.text: We analyzed the rate and form alignment of referentially aligned gestures across visibility conditions using Bayesian negative binomial regression models and Bayesian log-normal regression models, respectively.
As for the relation between the frequencies of lexical alignment and referentially aligned gestures, a Bayesian zero-inflated negative binomial regression model was used.
The models were fitted using the brms package (Version 2.22.0; Bürkner, 2018) in R (Version 4.2.2; R Core Team, 2024).
For the negative binomial regression models on the rate of referentially aligned gestures, we set an informative prior for the intercept: 𝑁𝑜𝑟𝑚𝑎𝑙(-1.39, 0.5).

This means that before seeing the data, we expected the most likely mean rate of referentially aligned gestures per iconic gesture to be 0.25 (𝑒𝑥𝑝(-1.39); one referentially aligned gesture per referents would therefore introduce additional variability that could obscure the effects of priming and grounding.
four iconic gestures on average), with the mean ranging from 0.09 (𝑒𝑥𝑝(-2.39)) to 0.68 (𝑒𝑥𝑝(-0.39)).

As for the zero-inflated negative binomial regression model on the relation between lexical alignment and referential alignment in gestures, we set an informative prior for the intercept as 𝑁𝑜𝑟𝑚𝑎𝑙(-1.2, 0.5), incorporating our prior expectation that the most likely mean frequency of referentially aligned gestures per trial would be 0.3 (𝑒𝑥𝑝(-1.2)) and that the mean would likely fall between 0.11 (𝑒𝑥𝑝(-2.2)) and 0.82 (𝑒𝑥𝑝(-0.2)).

These prior specifications are based on the results reported in Akamine et al. (2024) for data from Rasenberg et al. (2022), where pairs of Dutch-speaking participants performed the same referential communication task as ours but in a co-present setting.
text.formatted: These prior specifications are based on the results reported in <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Akamine et al. (2024)</ref> for data from <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Rasenberg et al. (2022)</ref>, where pairs of Dutch-speaking participants performed the same referential communication task as ours but in a co-present setting.

text.text: For the DTW distance, we set informative priors for the intercept as 𝑁𝑜𝑟𝑚𝑎𝑙(-0.7, 0.5), such that we expected the most likely mean DTW distance score to be 0.5 (𝑒𝑥𝑝(-0.7)) and that the mean to range from 0.18 (𝑒𝑥𝑝(-1.7)) to 1.35 (𝑒𝑥𝑝(0.3)).
To avoid biasing the slope estimates, we specified priors for 𝛽 as 𝑁𝑜𝑟𝑚𝑎𝑙(0, 0.2) or 𝑁𝑜𝑟𝑚𝑎𝑙(0, 0.5), depending on the fixed effects of interest.
Assigning 0 to 𝜇 of the prior distribution of 𝛽 means that before seeing the data, we expected the most likely mean slope estimate to be 0.
Setting 𝜇 to 0 when eliciting priors for the slope is a common way to avoid prejudging the direction of effects (Nicenboim et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Setting 𝜇 to 0 when eliciting priors for the slope is a common way to avoid prejudging the direction of effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Nicenboim et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: To perform hypothesis testing, we computed the Bayes factors using the Savage-Dickey density ratio method.

The Bayes factor is a measure of relative evidence of one model over the other, typically between the null model that does not contain the fixed effect of interest and the full model that contains the fixed effect of interest (BF10 ; Nicenboim et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The Bayes factor is a measure of relative evidence of one model over the other, typically between the null model that does not contain the fixed effect of interest and the full model that contains the fixed effect of interest (BF10 ; <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Nicenboim et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: One important advantage of Bayes factors is that "it is possible to find evidence for or against an effect.
This stands in contrast to the frequentist ANOVA which, in its standard usage, is designed to only furnish evidence against the null." (Schoknecht et al., 2025, p. 6).
text.formatted: This stands in contrast to the frequentist ANOVA which, in its standard usage, is designed to only furnish evidence against the null." <ref type="bibr">(Schoknecht et al., 2025, p. 6)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, hypothesis testing based on Bayes factors allows us to distinguish between evidence in favor of the alternative hypothesis, evidence in favor of the null hypothesis, and inconclusive evidence (e.g., due to noise or a limited number of observations).

As a stable estimation of the Bayes factor requires a large number of iterations, the models were run with four chains and 20,000 iterations per chain, with the initial 2000 iterations as the warm-up (Schad et al., 2023; Schoknecht et al., 2025).
text.formatted: As a stable estimation of the Bayes factor requires a large number of iterations, the models were run with four chains and 20,000 iterations per chain, with the initial 2000 iterations as the warm-up <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Schad et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Schoknecht et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, because the Bayes factor is sensitive to priors, we performed a sensitivity analysis by computing the Bayes factor for models with a range of priors with varying sizes of SD (Nicenboim et al., 2024; Schoknecht et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Furthermore, because the Bayes factor is sensitive to priors, we performed a sensitivity analysis by computing the Bayes factor for models with a range of priors with varying sizes of SD <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Nicenboim et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Schoknecht et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Bayes factors were interpreted based on Lee and Wagenmakers (2014)'s classification (see Figure 6).
text.formatted: Bayes factors were interpreted based on Lee and Wagenmakers (2014)'s classification (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">6</ref>).

text.text: To test whether the frequency of referentially aligned gestures produced by participant B differed across visibility conditions, we performed Bayesian hierarchical negative binomial regression models on participant B's rates of referentially aligned gestures per iconic gesture (i.e., the proportion of iconic gestures that were referentially aligned).

As mentioned in Section 2.3, we focused on analyzing gestural alignment established by participant B because comparing B's gestural alignment production across visibility conditions allowed us to investigate the effect of priming and grounding on gestural alignment.

We prepared a dataframe for the regression models, in which each row contained key attributes for a single trial, including dyad number, visibility condition, round number, trial number, target Fribble, and the frequencies of lexical alignment, iconic gestures, and referentially aligned gestures.

The total number of trials was 4320 (45 dyads * 96 trials), but we removed five trials that the participants accidentally skipped and 3051 trials (982 in SymAV, 1031 in AsymAV, 1038 in AO conditions) in which no iconic gesture was produced by participant Bfoot_3 .
text.formatted: The total number of trials was 4320 (45 dyads * 96 trials), but we removed five trials that the participants accidentally skipped and 3051 trials (982 in SymAV, 1031 in AsymAV, 1038 in AO conditions) in which no iconic gesture was produced by participant B<ref type="foot" target="#foot_3">foot_3</ref> .

text.text: The final dataframe consisted of 1264 rows (4320 trials -5 skipped trials -3051 trials with no iconic gestures produced by participant B).

We analyzed the rate of referentially aligned gestures with the negative binomial regression model, as it is suitable for modeling count data with no or unknown upper bound and estimates separate parameters for the mean and dispersion, unlike the Poisson regression model, which only estimates one parameter 𝜆 that determines both the mean and the variance of the data and assumes that mean = variance (Winter & Bürkner, 2021).

text.text: Note that negative binomial regressions use a log link as the canonical link function, so the coefficients are on the log scale and must be exponentiated to transform them back to the rate of referentially aligned gestures per iconic gesture.

Although previous research found no reliable effect of visibility on them in communicative interaction (Bavelas & Healing, 2013; Holler et al., 2011), we expected potential causal links, given that none of the previous studies included an asymmetric visibility condition.

In other words, the estimates reflect the effects flowing through the path of interest (Visibility → Mechanisms of Gestural Alignment → N. Gestural Alignment) and a path through gesturing (Visibility → N. Gestures → N. Gestural Alignment).

This means that, for example, if we observe a greater number of referentially aligned gestures in the SymAV condition than in the AO condition, we cannot determine if it is because mutual visibility increased the probability of alignment (Visibility → Mechanisms of Gestural Alignment → N. Gestural Alignment) or because people simply produced more gestures in the SymAV condition, resulting in an increased number of referentially aligned gestures (Visibility → N. Gestures → N. Gestural Alignment).

To solve this, we included the number of iconic gestures as a rate variable and modeled the rate of referentially aligned gestures per iconic gesture instead of raw frequency, ensuring that any differences in the rate of referentially aligned gestures across visibility conditions were not attributable to differences in the number of iconic gestures.
Conditioning on the number of iconic gestures created another problem known as the collider bias.

The collider bias is a form of selection bias that may distort causal estimation and occurs when conditioning on a variable commonly affected by two factors (McElreath, 2020; see Griffith et al., 2020 for a case study illustrating collider bias in understanding risk factors of COVID-19).
text.formatted: The collider bias is a form of selection bias that may distort causal estimation and occurs when conditioning on a variable commonly affected by two factors (McElreath, 2020; see <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Griffith et al., 2020</ref> for a case study illustrating collider bias in understanding risk factors of COVID-19).

text.text: In our causal model, we assumed that the frequency of iconic gestures would be affected by speaker visibility, the number of words, the role, and the round, and conditioning on the number of iconic gestures would generate collider biases (Visibility → N. Gestures ← Role → N. Gestural Alignment; Visibility → N. Gestures ← Round → N. Gestural Alignment).
To tackle this issue, we added the role and round as fixed effects.
We applied contrast coding to the visibility condition and rounds.
The visibility condition was backward-difference coded, allowing us to compare the means of adjacent levels: AO-AsymAV and AsymAV-SymAV.
We also applied backward-difference coding to the round variable so that we could estimate the difference between R1 and R², R² and R3, and so forth.

We used an ordered categorical round variable instead of a continuous one (e.g., centered round) because the change in the rate of referentially aligned gestures across rounds did not follow a linear pattern.

In summary, to estimate the causal effect of speaker visibility on the frequency of referentially aligned gestures, we modeled the rate of referentially aligned gestures with a Bayesian hierarchical negative binomial regression model with centered number of iconic gestures as an exposure variable and fixed effects for the visibility condition, round, and role, and the interaction between the visibility condition and the round.
As for the random effects, we included by-dyad varying intercepts plus slopes for the round, along with by-item varying intercepts.

We are also interested in estimating the association between the frequencies of lexical alignment and referentially aligned gestures.

To this end, we fitted a separate Bayesian hierarchical zero-inflated negative binomial regression model, with the visibility condition, round, role, and centered number of iconic gestures as fixed effects.

Here, we included the number of iconic gestures as a fixed effect rather than an exposure variable to ensure that lexical alignment and referentially aligned gestures are on the same scale, without introducing confounding.

In other words, modeling the frequency of referentially aligned gestures per iconic gesture as a function of the lexical alignment rate per iconic gesture introduces a spurious correlation because both variables would be influenced by the number of gestures (N. Lexical Alignment ← N. Gestures → N. Gestural Alignment).

To test whether referentially aligned gestures differ in form similarity across visibility conditions, we fit Bayesian hierarchical log-normal regression models to the DTW distance scores.
We chose log-normal regression models over linear regression models because the DTW distance scores are positively skewed and can range from 0 to ∞.

We also compared the predictive performance of linear regression and log-normal regression models using (approximate) leave-one-out cross-validation (McElreath, 2020; Vasishth et al., 2018; Winter & Bürkner, 2021) and found that the log-normal model was associated with a higher predictive power (difference in expected log pointwise predictive density = 27.1) and a lower standard error (difference = -11.1).

Research has shown that linguistic alignment occurs not only in speech but also in co-speech gestures (e.g., Akamine et al., 2024; Oben & Brône, 2016; Rasenberg et al., 2020), and that it is driven by two major processes: priming and grounding (Rasenberg et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Research has shown that linguistic alignment occurs not only in speech but also in co-speech gestures (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Akamine et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Oben & Brône, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Rasenberg et al., 2020)</ref>, and that it is driven by two major processes: priming and grounding <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Rasenberg et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: While these processes have been extensively studied in verbal language use, experimental evidence for their role in gestural alignment remains limited.
Furthermore, several studies have proposed that speech and gesture alignment are likely integrated (e.g., Kopp & Bergmann, 2013), yet the exact nature of this relationship has not been established.
text.formatted: Furthermore, several studies have proposed that speech and gesture alignment are likely integrated (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Kopp & Bergmann, 2013)</ref>, yet the exact nature of this relationship has not been established.

text.text: To address these gaps, we examined how speaker visibility in video-mediated repeated-reference games affects gestural alignment, focusing on the effects of priming and grounding on referential and form alignment of iconic gestures.
We also investigated the relationship between lexical and gestural alignment, specifically, whether lexical alignment is associated with referential alignment in gestures.

We found that seeing a partner's gestures increased referential alignment, whereas mutual visibility (both seeing and being seen by one's partner) did not provide evidence of an additional increase in referential alignment.
In contrast, visibility had little to no effect on the form similarity of referentially aligned gestures.
Finally, the frequency of lexical alignment was positively associated with that of referentially aligned gestures.

Together, these findings highlight the importance of distinguishing between referential and form alignment when investigating the mechanisms underlying gestural alignment and suggest a relationship between alignment in speech and gesture.
We discuss these findings in detail below.

We found that speaker visibility is associated with the rate of referential alignment in gestures: Participants were more likely to align with their conversation partner's gestures if they could see their partner's gestures (SymAV and AsymAV) compared to when they could not see each other (AO), but the visibility of their own gestures to their partner did not affect the rate of referentially aligned gestures (SymAV = AsymAV > AO).
text.formatted: We found that speaker visibility is associated with the rate of referential alignment in gestures: Participants were more likely to align with their conversation partner's gestures if they could see their partner's gestures (SymAV and AsymAV) compared to when they could not see each other (AO), but the visibility of their own gestures to their partner did not affect the rate of referentially aligned gestures (SymAV = AsymAV > AO).

text.text: These results suggest that gesture-to-gesture priming is likely one of the factors driving referential alignment in gestures, while there was limited evidence that people strategically produce referentially aligned gestures as a communicative resource for grounding.

How can we explain the limited effect of grounding in our data, given that previous research has shown that people align in gestures in the process of grounding (e.g., Chui, 2014; Holler & Wilkin, 2011; Rasenberg et al., 2022)?
text.formatted: How can we explain the limited effect of grounding in our data, given that previous research has shown that people align in gestures in the process of grounding (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Chui, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Holler & Wilkin, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Rasenberg et al., 2022)</ref>?

text.text: One possibility is that gestural alignment can yield communicative benefits without necessarily being produced for the listener.

In other words, speakers may produce aligned gestures due to priming or non-interdependent factors, but these gestures can nevertheless convey semantic information and facilitate listeners' comprehension, regardless of whether the speakers intended them to be informative for the listeners or not.

This is consistent with previous findings that gesture rates do not always reliably differ depending on whether speakers see each other (Bavelas & Healing, 2013; Holler et al., 2011), suggesting that speakers continue to produce gestures even when they are not informative to the listeners.
text.formatted: This is consistent with previous findings that gesture rates do not always reliably differ depending on whether speakers see each other <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bavelas & Healing, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Holler et al., 2011)</ref>, suggesting that speakers continue to produce gestures even when they are not informative to the listeners.

text.text: Another possibility is that participant B in the AsymAV condition sometimes forgot that they were not visible to their partner, leading them to behave more like participants in the SymAV condition.
If so, both priming and grounding could have contributed to referential alignment in gestures in the AsymAV condition.

Although we attempted to minimize this possibility by displaying the self-view throughout the entire interaction, we cannot rule it out, especially because such asymmetrical visibility is relatively rare in video-mediated dialogue and has only recently been introduced in social interactions.
However, it seems implausible that all participants in the AsymAV consistently forgot that they were not visible to their partner.

If grounding also contributes to referential alignment in gestures, we would expect some difference between the SymAV and AsymAV conditions unless a majority of participant Bs consistently forgot about their visibility.

Therefore, a more plausible explanation for our finding is that seeing a partner's gestures primes the production of referentially aligned gestures, while the additional contribution of the grounding process may be limited.
Another noteworthy finding is that even when participants could not see each other, they produced referentially aligned gestures at a rate of 24%.
In the SymAV and AsymAV conditions, this rate was approximately 38%.

This increased rate of alignment from the AO to the AsymAV conditions represented about 37% of referentially aligned gestures observed in the B (Director) -Round 1 Maar dan zijn snavel zijn twee van die blokken aan de voorkant.

AsymAV condition.

Because rates were similar between the SymAV and AsymAV conditions, approximately one-third of the referentially aligned gestures observed in the SymAV and AsymAV conditions may be attributable to gesture-to-gesture priming.
Importantly, the remaining two-thirds of referentially aligned gestures observed cannot be accounted for by the additional contribution of seeing a partner's gestures or by mutual visibility.
This suggests that gesture-to-gesture priming and grounding, as operationalized in our study, may not fully account for the production of referentially aligned gestures.

These results therefore argue for moving beyond the dichotomous view of alignment mechanisms and considering other processes that may contribute to linguistic alignment, such as conceptual commonality and cross-modal interplay.
Taken together, these findings suggest that gesture-to-gesture priming is a mechanism underlying referential alignment in co-speech gestures.
Inconsistent with our prediction, speaker visibility did not influence the level of gesture form similarity for referentially aligned gestures.

This result suggests that seeing gestures may not enhance gesture form similarity and may not be necessary for producing gestures that resemble those previously produced by their conversation partners.
This finding has three implications for theories of gestural alignment.

First, the finding that gesture form similarity was not reliably higher in the AsymAV condition than in the AO condition suggests that automatic low-level motor priming does not contribute to higher gesture form similarity in the repeated-reference game.
One potential reason for the null effect relates to the nature of our task.

The majority of lexical alignment and referentially aligned gestures observed in our dataset occurred across rounds, such that participants tended to reuse word choices and gestures that were produced by their partner in the previous round, presumably to refer to the object more efficiently.
As participants had to communicate about 16 objects in each round, the priming effect on the gesture form may have faded away by the time they had to describe the object (see Appendix A).
This explanation is reasonable because holding the exact form of many gestures in working memory seems cognitively taxing.

Given that we observed a more prominent priming effect on the referential alignment in gestures, it may be that the effects of semantic priming of the referent depicted in gesture (meaning) are stronger or more persistent than motor-spatial priming of the gesture itself (form).
Second, the fact that there was no difference in DTW distance between the AsymAV and SymAV conditions suggests that grounding may not necessarily lead to higher alignment in gesture form.
This is in line with the idea that the necessity for grounding could sometimes lead to higher alignment in gesture form and at other times lead to strategic (partial) misalignment in gesture form.

For instance, people may sometimes produce similar gestures to signal understanding, but they can also produce gestures that are different from their partner's to negotiate how to conceptualize the referent (Rasenberg et al., 2022).
text.formatted: For instance, people may sometimes produce similar gestures to signal understanding, but they can also produce gestures that are different from their partner's to negotiate how to conceptualize the referent <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Rasenberg et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Third, the example in Figure 10 nicely illustrates that gesture form reflects the speaker's conceptualization of the referent.
text.formatted: Third, the example in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_8">10</ref> nicely illustrates that gesture form reflects the speaker's conceptualization of the referent.

text.text: In the example, participant B produced an iconic gesture depicting the "beak of the bird that is made of two of those blocks", while participant A produced an iconic gesture depicting "two protruding things".
The participants produced two distinct iconic gestures because they conceptualized the referent differently.
In particular, speaker B conceptualized the object as a bird, while speaker A conceptualized it as an object with two protruding bars.
This discrepancy in their conceptualizations may have resulted in two distinct gestures.
In contrast, if they both conceptualized the referent as the "beak" of a bird, they might have produced more similar-looking gestures.

This is in line with the notion that gestures serve as a "window into the mind" (McNeill, 2005) and with the previous finding that conceptual commonality plays a role in the repetition of gesture form features (Dingemanse, 2015; Mol et al., 2012).
text.formatted: This is in line with the notion that gestures serve as a "window into the mind" <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(McNeill, 2005)</ref> and with the previous finding that conceptual commonality plays a role in the repetition of gesture form features <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Dingemanse, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Mol et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: This account also explains why participants in the AO condition could produce gestures at a similar level of form similarity as in the other conditions.
As long as they align in the conceptualization of the referent, they are likely to be able to achieve some level of gesture form similarity.

In summary, our findings suggest that observing gestures may not always lead to higher similarity in gesture form across repeated references, but rather, conceptual similarity may play a key role in driving form alignment in referentially aligned gestures.

More than a decade ago, Kopp and Bergmann (2013) introduced an integrated model of speech and gesture production and perception, which attempted to systematically model the automatic and strategic alignment of co-speech gestures in dialogue.
text.formatted: More than a decade ago, <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Kopp and Bergmann (2013)</ref> introduced an integrated model of speech and gesture production and perception, which attempted to systematically model the automatic and strategic alignment of co-speech gestures in dialogue.

text.text: They, along with others like Pickering and Garrod (2021), speculated about the interaction between the production and perception of speech and co-speech gestures and the interaction between alignment in speech and gestures.
text.formatted: They, along with others like <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Pickering and Garrod (2021)</ref>, speculated about the interaction between the production and perception of speech and co-speech gestures and the interaction between alignment in speech and gestures.

text.text: However, the nature of these interactions has been underexplored.
To address this gap, we investigated the relationship between the frequencies of lexical alignment and referentially aligned gestures.
Our results indicate that the frequency of lexical alignment is positively associated with the frequency of referentially aligned gestures, even when accounting for other relevant variables.
Therefore, we argue that lexical and gestural alignment are closely connected.

This aligns with the observation that the emergence of multimodal alignment (lexical + gestural) is much more frequent than the emergence of lexical-only or gestural-only alignment (Rasenberg et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This aligns with the observation that the emergence of multimodal alignment (lexical + gestural) is much more frequent than the emergence of lexical-only or gestural-only alignment <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Rasenberg et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: It is also consistent with the claims that speech and gestures are interrelated (e.g., Kita and Özyürek (2003)'s Interface Model) and that alignment at one level leads to alignment at other levels (Interactive Alignment Model; Pickering & Garrod, 2004).
text.formatted: It is also consistent with the claims that speech and gestures are interrelated (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Kita and Özyürek (2003)</ref>'s Interface Model) and that alignment at one level leads to alignment at other levels (Interactive Alignment Model; <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Pickering & Garrod, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: What could cause the association between lexical alignment and referential alignment in gestures?

We propose that lexical alignment and referential alignment in gestures both reflect alignment of conceptual representations, which is shaped by preceding words and gestures (words/gestures → alignment of conceptual representations → lexical/gestural alignment).
Imagine that in the audio-only condition, speaker A describes Fribble 09 as "this object has a long nose like Pinocchio" (gesturing the nose, which B cannot see).

After hearing this description, speaker B may construe the object as Pinocchio as well, so in the next round, B is more likely to describe the object as Pinocchio and gesture about its salient feature, the nose (see Figure 11).
text.formatted: After hearing this description, speaker B may construe the object as Pinocchio as well, so in the next round, B is more likely to describe the object as Pinocchio and gesture about its salient feature, the nose (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_9">11</ref>).

text.text: Here, A's speech led B to align in how to conceptualize the object, which in turn led B to use the same word and gesture about the same referent.
On this account, not only gestures but also words can influence referential alignment in gestures, via alignment of conceptual representations.

This proposal is consistent with the Interactive Alignment Model's claim that alignment at the lexical representation level leads to alignment at the semantic and conceptual representation levels (Pickering & Garrod, 2004), and extends the proposal by suggesting that such spreading can reach the gestures.
text.formatted: This proposal is consistent with the Interactive Alignment Model's claim that alignment at the lexical representation level leads to alignment at the semantic and conceptual representation levels <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Pickering & Garrod, 2004)</ref>, and extends the proposal by suggesting that such spreading can reach the gestures.

text.text: It is also consistent with a previous claim that alignment in gesture form reflects conceptual convergence (Mol et al., 2012).
text.formatted: It is also consistent with a previous claim that alignment in gesture form reflects conceptual convergence <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Mol et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Because we did not manipulate or measure conceptual alignment, this proposal remains to be tested in future research.

Having identified an association between lexical alignment and referential alignment in gestures, we next consider its effect size and how it relates to the observed effect of gesture-to-gesture priming.
Overall, cross-modal associations represented 16.3% of referentially aligned gestures.

Given that approximately 37.8% of referentially aligned gestures in the SymAV and AsymAV conditions were explained by gesture-to-gesture priming, approximately half (16.3% + 37.8% = 54.1%) of referentially aligned gestures can be attributed to priming and cross-modal association.
Future research is needed to investigate additional factors underlying the remaining half of referentially aligned gestures, including the visual saliency and complexity of stimuli.
In sum, these findings suggest that alignment in word choices and alignment in gestures are closely linked.
We propose that this association may reflect alignment in the speakers' conceptual representations of the referent, which is partly shaped by preceding words and gestures.

We conducted an experiment in which participants repeatedly communicated about novel objects on Zoom with varying speaker visibilities and demonstrated that priming partly drives referential alignment in co-speech gestures, while the effects of grounding may be rather limited.
We also found that neither priming nor grounding strongly affects form alignment in referentially aligned gestures.
Lastly, we showed that lexical alignment and referential alignment in gestures are linked.
To what extent can these findings be generalized to co-present face-to-face interaction?
We speculate on the generalizability to face-to-face interaction, drawing on a recent study that compared multimodal language production in face-to-face and Zoom interactions (Akamine et al., 2025).
text.formatted: We speculate on the generalizability to face-to-face interaction, drawing on a recent study that compared multimodal language production in face-to-face and Zoom interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Akamine et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Some of the key findings in the paper related to linguistic alignment were that (i) the lexical alignment rate at the start of Zoom interactions is significantly lower than that of face-to-face interactions, (ii) the rate of referentially aligned gestures remains consistent across both communicative settings, and (iii) the degree of gesture form similarity is significantly higher in Zoom interactions compared to face-to-face interactions.
Based on these results, we propose that our findings on the frequency of referentially aligned gestures are likely generalizable to face-to-face interaction.

Regarding gesture form similarity, we expect generally lower gesture form similarity in face-to-face contexts; however, it is unlikely that the effect of visibility differs across the communicative settings.
In sum, we believe that our findings can be generalized well to face-to-face interaction.

This study investigated the mechanisms of gestural alignment by manipulating the visibility of speakers in video-mediated interactions, thereby allowing us to examine the effects of automatic priming and strategic grounding on referential and form alignment in co-speech gestures.
Our findings revealed that seeing a conversation partner's gestures, but not the visibility of one's own gestures to the partner, enhances the likelihood of referential alignment in iconic gestures.
This provides experimental evidence for gesture-to-gesture priming, while offering no clear evidence of an additional contribution of grounding to referential alignment.
In contrast, the visibility manipulation did not reliably affect the form similarity of referentially aligned gestures.

These results suggest that referential and form alignment may involve different mechanisms, underscoring the importance of distinguishing between these dimensions when investigating gestural alignment.
Furthermore, the study investigated the relationship between frequencies of lexical alignment and referentially aligned gestures, and identified a likely connection between them.

We propose that this association may reflect between-speaker convergence in the conceptual representation of the referent, potentially facilitated by the words and gestures produced by one's conversation partner (Poncelet-Romaneli et al., 2025).
text.formatted: We propose that this association may reflect between-speaker convergence in the conceptual representation of the referent, potentially facilitated by the words and gestures produced by one's conversation partner <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Poncelet-Romaneli et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This contributes to our understanding of the relationship between alignment in the vocal and bodily modalities.
In conclusion, this research highlights the importance of considering both automatic and strategic processes when investigating linguistic alignment across different levels and modalities.
It also demonstrates the value of experimentally examining the contributions of these processes while distinguishing between different dimensions of alignment.

Taken together, we found no indication that the temporal distance masked a visibility effect on form alignment.

However, the relatively small number of within-trial gesture pairs and the inconclusive evidence for the interaction mean that we cannot rule out the possibility that visibility effects vary with temporal lag.
Further research with more data is needed to investigate this possibility.

The majority of referentially aligned gesture pairs occurred across rounds (n = 815 gesture pairs; 83% of referentially aligned gestures; median lag = 3 min 44 s), whereas within-trial alignment was relatively rare (n = 171 gesture pairs; 17% of referentially aligned gestures; median lag = 6.02 s).
Overall, the median temporal lag between the first and second gestures in a referentially aligned pair was relatively long (3 min 19 s).
Such long lags may have weakened the visibility effects on gesture form alignment.

To investigate whether visibility effects on form alignment varied with temporal lag, we extended the form alignment analysis by adding lag category (across rounds vs. within the same trial) as a predictor, including its interaction with visibility.
We categorized referentially aligned gesture pairs as either within-trial or across rounds.
We used treatment coding, with across rounds as the reference category.
As in the main analysis, we modeled DTW distance for referentially aligned gesture pairs using a Bayesian hierarchical log-normal regression model.
Because there were relatively few within-trial pairs, we excluded centered round and its interaction with visibility from the fixed effects.
